summary:
vLLM's weight storage CAN be replaced after load — the primitive already exists and is used routinely. `replace_parameter()` (two variants) re-registers a brand-new `torch.nn.Parameter` whenever dtype/shape/storage-size changes, and Marlin repacking already does exactly a size-AND-dtype-changing swap (fp8 (n,k) -> packed int32) inside `process_weights_after_loading`. So a K3->K4 re-encode is representable in the parameter system.

The blocker is not the parameter system — it is WHEN. Every existing size-changing swap happens during startup, strictly before CUDA graph capture (`base_loader.py:74` load, then `gpu_worker.py:608` capture). vLLM does ship a genuine runtime weight-reload path (`reload_weights` collective RPC, plus a `reload/` layerwise package added for RLHF weight sync), but that path DELIBERATELY forbids storage replacement: after re-running `process_weights_after_loading`, it copies results back into the ORIGINAL kernel tensors (`layerwise.py:244-246`) and re-registers the ORIGINAL Parameter objects (`layerwise.py:267-275`), with the comment "preserves cudagraph refs". So the EPLB fixed-shape asymmetry the user identified applies verbatim to the reload path too — it is baked in by design, not an oversight.

Three findings materially help the idea beyond what was assumed: (1) online BF16->fp8/MXFP8 quantization at startup ALREADY EXISTS as a first-class layer-at-a-time meta-device path (`uses_meta_device`, `Fp8OnlineLinearMethod`, `Mxfp8OnlineMoEMethod`), and is explicitly designed to RE-RUN during reload (`layerwise.py:219-222` deletes the already-processed guard); (2) selective per-layer reload of a SUBSET of tensors is already supported — untouched layers are restored verbatim (`layerwise.py:192-193`); (3) safetensors access is per-tensor random access via `safe_open`/`get_tensor`, so JIT-fetching one re-encoded expert is feasible. What does NOT exist is any disk cache of online-quantized weights, and the one save path that exists is TP-rank-baked, conflicting with the "topology neutral" goal.

claims.claim: vLLM already has a primitive that replaces a parameter's underlying STORAGE with a different size and dtype after load. `vllm/model_executor/utils.py:47` unconditionally builds a new `torch.nn.Parameter(new_data)` and `setattr`s it, preserving `weight_loader`. The sibling `layer_utils.py:22` variant takes an in-place fast path ONLY when type, dtype and `untyped_storage().nbytes()` all match, and otherwise falls back to `mod.register_parameter(name, torch.nn.Parameter(new))`. A K3->K4 size change simply takes the fallback branch.

claims.claim: Marlin repacking is an existing, in-tree precedent for a parameter swap that changes BOTH tensor size and dtype during `process_weights_after_loading` — the closest analogue to a bit-width re-encode. It takes an fp8 weight of shape (part_size_k, part_size_n), packs it to int32, calls `ops.gptq_marlin_repack`, and replaces the parameter with a differently-shaped int32 tensor.

claims.claim: `process_weights_after_loading` is invoked exactly once per module at startup, from inside `BaseModelLoader.load_model`, immediately after `load_weights` and before the model is returned. There is no periodic or scheduled re-invocation anywhere in the normal serving loop.

claims.claim: CUDA graph capture happens strictly AFTER all weight loading and post-processing, during `compile_or_warm_up_model`. This is why every existing size-changing swap is safe: it completes before any graph exists.

claims.claim: BLOCKER for naive hot-swap: replacing a weight's storage after CUDA graph capture silently corrupts execution, and vLLM will NOT detect it. The replay guard records and asserts only the `data_ptr()` of tensors passed as *args* to the captured callable — weight pointers baked into the captured kernel launch parameters are never validated.

claims.workaround: Three options: (a) run `enforce_eager=True` and eat the throughput loss; (b) re-capture CUDA graphs after each swap (expensive, and capture requires quiescing the engine); (c) follow the reload design and keep the pointer stable — which forbids size changes. Option (c) is what vLLM chose.

claims.claim: vLLM DOES have a runtime weight-replacement path already: a `reload_weights` collective RPC on the worker, backed by a dedicated `model_loader/reload/` package that puts layers back on the meta device, re-runs the real weight loaders, re-runs quantization, and finalizes. This is far more machinery than 'vLLM loads weights once at startup' implies.

claims.workaround: Reuse this as the transport skeleton. It already handles meta-device round-tripping, loader wrapping, and per-layer progress accounting.

claims.claim: BLOCKER as-is: the reload path is hard-wired to same-shape, same-dtype, same-pointer replacement. After re-running `process_weights_after_loading`, `_layerwise_process` copies the processed values back into the pre-existing kernel tensors with `param.data.copy_(...)`, then `_place_kernel_tensors` re-registers the ORIGINAL Parameter objects. A K3->K4 tensor would fail the `copy_` on element-count mismatch. The inline comment states the reason: 'preserves cudagraph refs'.
claims.evidence: vllm/model_executor/model_loader/reload/layerwise.py:240-246 (comment at :240, param.data.copy_ at :244, buffer copy at :246); _place_kernel_tensors at :267-275 (delattr then re-register the saved originals); originals saved at :96
claims.workaround: This is the exact EPLB asymmetry, now confirmed in the reload path. To change size you must skip the copy-back, let `replace_parameter` re-register, AND invalidate/re-capture CUDA graphs. Alternatively over-allocate every expert at max bit-width (K4) and vary only the *populated* prefix, keeping storage nbytes constant — that makes the fast path legal at the cost of losing the memory saving that motivates the idea.

claims.claim: Selective reload of a SUBSET of tensors IS already supported at layer granularity. `reload_weights` accepts an arbitrary `weights_iterator`, and layers that receive no weights are restored untouched from their saved kernel tensors; only layers that reached their expected element count get materialized, processed, and copied back.

claims.workaround: Feed a generator yielding only the experts being rebalanced. Bookkeeping is O(all modules) but materialization and re-quantization are O(touched layers) — well matched to periodic incremental rebalancing.

claims.claim: Online quantization from a BF16 checkpoint ALREADY EXISTS as a first-class, memory-efficient, layer-at-a-time path. `QuantizeMethodBase.uses_meta_device` marks methods that create weights on the meta device and quantize during `process_weights_after_loading`. FP8 and MXFP8 both implement it for linear and MoE. Weights are created on meta, materialized just-in-time inside a patched weight loader, and quantized the instant the layer's element count is complete — so peak memory holds only one BF16 layer at a time.

claims.claim: The online-quantization path is explicitly designed to RE-RUN during a weight reload. `Fp8OnlineLinearMethod` guards against double work with `layer._already_called_process_weights_after_loading`, and the reload code deliberately deletes that attribute so quantization re-executes on the freshly loaded BF16 weights.

claims.claim: There is NO disk cache of online-quantized weights. Nothing in `vllm/model_executor/` writes quantized results to disk during or after load. The only weight-writing paths are the user-invoked `ShardedStateLoader.save_model` and a .bin->safetensors converter.

claims.claim: The existing save path is TP-topology-baked, directly conflicting with the 'topology neutral' requirement: filenames are formatted with the tensor-parallel rank, and the saved tensors are per-rank shards of already-processed kernel-format weights.

claims.claim: HAZARD: `FusedMoEQuantConfig` is memoized on the quant method and captures DIRECT tensor references to scale/bias parameters. Swapping any of those parameters after the first forward leaves the cached config pointing at the stale tensor, with no invalidation hook.

claims.claim: In eager execution, `apply()` resolves weights by attribute lookup on the layer at call time, so a rebound parameter IS picked up immediately. The immutability requirement comes from graph capture, not from the quant-method interface.

claims.workaround: `enforce_eager=True` makes atomic rebinding viable today, at a real decode-throughput cost — a reasonable first prototype gate before tackling graph re-capture.

claims.claim: `BasevLLMParameter` subclasses carry loading metadata (weight_loader, tp_rank, tp_size, input_dim/output_dim, packing factors) that is NOT automatically transferred when a parameter is replaced; existing code copies it explicitly. A re-encode that swaps parameter objects must reconstruct these or later reloads break.
claims.evidence: vllm/model_executor/parameter.py:31-85 (BasevLLMParameter, weight_loader property/setter/deleter at :67-85, tp_rank/tp_size at :64-65); explicit __dict__ preservation in reload at reload/meta.py:36-38 and :52-54; _copy_missing_attrs at fp8.py:557 and :617; weight_loader preservation at vllm/model_executor/utils.py:72-75

claims.claim: EPLB does provide reusable scaffolding for the periodic decision loop: a configurable step interval with randomized phase offset, and a `step()` hook already wired into the serving loop.

claims.claim: Per-tensor random access to safetensors is already used, so fetching a single named re-encoded tensor on demand (rather than streaming whole shards) is supported by the existing I/O layer.

verdicts.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not. The cited evidence says exactly what the agent thinks, and the claim is UNDERSTATED in four independent ways.

=== THE CITED CODE IS ACCURATE ===

/home/user/vllm-voipmonitor/vllm/compilation/cuda_graph.py:276-279 (capture):
    input_addresses = [x.data_ptr() for x in args if isinstance(x, torch.Tensor)]
    entry.input_addresses = input_addresses
:340-347 (replay):
    new_input_addresses = [x.data_ptr() for x in args if isinstance(x, torch.Tensor)]
    assert new_input_addresses == entry.input_addresses, ...

Weights are not in `args`. They are module attributes reached through the closure `self.runnable` (invoked at :311 inside `torch.cuda.graph`). Their addresses are burned into the captured kernel launch parameters and are never recorded, so nothing can compare them. `grep -rn "input_addresses|data_ptr" vllm/compilation/` returns ONLY these two sites — there is no second guard anywhere in the compilation stack.

=== WORSE THAN STATED (1): the guard is dead code in production ===
The assert is gated at :338 on `self.is_debugging_mode`, set at :191 to `envs.VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL == "DEBUG"`. Default is "INFO" (vllm/envs.py:40 and :676). There is no independent flag to enable it. So in a normal serving process, even the *argument* pointers are unchecked. The docstring at :166-167 admits this ("guaranteed when VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL == 'DEBUG'").

=== WORSE THAN STATED (2): kwargs are excluded ===
Both comprehensions iterate `args` only. A tensor passed by keyword is unvalidated even in DEBUG mode.

=== WORSE THAN STATED (3): a second capture path with ZERO guard ===
/home/user/vllm-voipmonitor/vllm/v1/worker/gpu_ubatch_wrapper.py:243-273 captures its own `torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()` for microbatched/DBO execution, stores it in `self.cudagraphs[num_tokens]`, and replays at :486. It records no addresses at all — not even the DEBUG-mode check. Any hot-swap scheme must handle this path too.

=== WORSE THAN STATED (4): the canonical quant-weight-swap helper does exactly the unsafe thing ===
/home/user/vllm-voipmonitor/vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/utils/layer_utils.py:20-40, `replace_parameter()` — used 143 times across vllm/, it is THE mechanism quant methods use to swap in a re-packed weight:
    if type(old) is type(new) and old.dtype == new.dtype and old.untyped_storage().nbytes() == new.untyped_storage().nbytes():
        update_tensor_inplace(old, new)      # preserves data_ptr
    else:
        mod.register_parameter(name, torch.nn.Parameter(new, ...))   # NEW storage, NEW data_ptr
A K3->K4 change differs in nbytes by construction, so it takes the else branch unconditionally. No cudagraph invalidation exists on that path. It is safe today only because it runs during load, before capture.

=== DECISIVE: vLLM's own runtime weight-update path confirms the hazard ===
vLLM DOES support live weight replacement (the RLHF path), and it is engineered specifically around this constraint:
- /home/user/vllm-voipmonitor/vllm/model_executor/model_loader/reload/layerwise.py:240 — verbatim comment: "# Copy processed values into original tensor storage (preserves cudagraph refs)", followed at :244 by `param.data.copy_(getattr(layer, name))`.
- :267-275 `_place_kernel_tensors` deletes and re-registers the SAME saved Parameter objects, so storage identity survives.
- /home/user/vllm-voipmonitor/vllm/v1/worker/gpu_model_runner.py:4725 logs "Reloading weights inplace..."; :4746 `param.copy_(loaded_weight)`.
- /home/user/vllm-voipmonitor/vllm/v1/worker/gpu_worker.py:1006 `param.copy_(weight)`.
This is first-party acknowledgment that (a) cudagraphs bake weight pointers, (b) nothing validates them, and (c) the only sanctioned mitigation is to never change the pointer. Critically, `copy_` cannot change nbytes/dtype — so the one supported live-update path structurally CANNOT express a K3->K4 bit-width change. This directly reinforces the project's stated EPLB asymmetry.

=== ESCAPE HATCHES I FOUND (they weaken "no mitigation exists", NOT the claim) ===
1. `CUDAGraphWrapper.clear_all_graphs()` (cuda_graph.py:172-176, 227-228) exists, but its only caller is memory profiling inside capture_model (gpu_model_runner.py:5694), immediately after `set_cudagraph_capturing_enabled(False)` at :5693. No runtime/API path re-captures graphs after a weight change. Re-capture would also need the dispatcher keys rebuilt (:5698-5700).
2. CuMemAllocator (/home/user/vllm-voipmonitor/vllm/device_allocator/cumem.py:199-250) is the most promising precedent for the proposal: `sleep()` calls `unmap_and_release(handle)` to free PHYSICAL pages while `wake_up()` calls `create_and_map(handle)` to remap at the SAME virtual `ptr`. That is genuinely "swap the bytes under a stable pointer," which is why sleep/wake does not corrupt captured graphs. But the reservation size `handle[1]` is fixed, so it cannot express a bit-width change either — unless you over-reserve VA at max bpw and leave the tail unmapped, which is the architecturally correct route but is not implemented and is not what "naive hot-swap" means.
3. `CUDAGraphMode.NONE` (cuda_graph.py:241-251) bypasses capture entirely — a real escape hatch at large throughput cost.

None of these refute the claim; they confirm that the safe designs all pin either the pointer or the size, and a fungible-quant scheme changes both. Failure mode is also worth flagging: a freed/reallocated storage does not fault, it reads whatever now occupies that address, so the corruption is silent garbage output rather than a crash.

summary:
vLLM (at 99267c23) has six live, shipped mechanisms that mutate model weights or model memory after startup: (1) EPLB expert rearrangement, (2) the RLHF weight-transfer / reload_weights path, (3) sleep mode's CuMemAllocator, (4) Elastic EP rescaling, (5) LoRA adapter slots, and (6) the PrefetchOffloader weight streamer. Every one of them is precedent for the "fungible quant" idea, but exactly one of them (LoRA) is designed for a variable-sized payload, and it handles it by padding into a fixed max-size slot.

The single most important finding is the EPLB invariant: EPLB NEVER changes a tensor's shape, dtype, size, or address. Its scratch buffer is literally `torch.empty_like(w)` (rebalance_execute.py:608-610), every movement is `dst_row.copy_(src_row)` on identically-shaped rows, and its P2P ops send/recv the same `w[src]`/`b[dst]` slices. Worse for the proposal: `FusedMoE.get_expert_weights()` returns `weight.view(local_num_experts, -1)` (fused_moe/layer.py:1441-1449), so all experts in a layer are rows of ONE contiguous tensor with a uniform per-expert stride. Per-expert K3-vs-K4 heterogeneity within a layer is not "hard" in this layout — it is structurally unrepresentable. Per-LAYER heterogeneity is merely hard.

The second most important finding cuts the other way, and it's good news: CuMemAllocator DOES use CUDA VMM exactly as hoped. `cuMemAddressReserve` (csrc/cumem_allocator.cpp:323) reserves a virtual range; sleep() calls `cuMemUnmap`+`cuMemRelease` (cumem.py:214 -> cpp:207,211) but deliberately does NOT call `cuMemAddressFree` (that only happens in my_free, cpp:528); wake_up() re-runs `cuMemCreate`+`cuMemMap` at the SAME `d_mem` (cumem.py:241 -> cpp:130,145). So "stable virtual address while the physical backing is torn down and rebuilt" is already a shipped, production capability in vLLM. The gap is that the size is frozen: the handle tuple carries one `alignedSize` fixed at malloc time (cpp:319), and both unmap and map use it. Making the backing size variable needs new C, not a new concept.

Three other findings materially de-risk the proposal. First, runtime RE-QUANTIZATION already exists: the layerwise reload path re-runs `quant_method.process_weights_after_loading(layer)` on a live layer (reload/layerwise.py:236-238), including the meta-device round-trip that deletes and re-registers a layer's parameters (reload/meta.py:76-104). Second, `update_tensor_inplace` (quantization/utils/layer_utils.py:8-17) mutates a live tensor's shape AND stride in place via `as_strided_` while keeping data_ptr — the one in-tree primitive that changes a tensor's logical shape without changing its address. Third, Elastic EP already performs the full nuclear option at runtime: it drops `model.expert_weights`, rebuilds quant_method and the modular kernel runner, then calls `torch.compiler.reset()` and re-runs `compile_or_warm_up_model()` to re-capture all CUDA graphs (elastic_execute.py:356-372, 405-414).

The honest architectural read: the proposal cannot be built as "EPLB but for bits." EPLB's transport layer is the wrong precedent — it is a fixed-shape row shuffler. The right composite is LoRA's max-size-slot padding + the PrefetchOffloader's static buffer pool and CUDA-graph-safe H2D streaming + layerwise reload's re-quantize-and-rebind + sleep mode's stable-VA remapping, with EPLB contributing only its cadence model (one layer per engine step, threading.Lock plus two CUDA events) and its profile-run memory reservation trick.

Separately, and this may be the real blocker for the user's stated "hard part": there is no in-tree signal that could drive the upgrade/downgrade decision. `expert_load_view.scatter_add_(..., src=torch.ones_like(topk_ids_flatten))` (fused_moe/router/base_router.py:81-84) counts token routings and nothing else. vLLM records how OFTEN an expert fires, never how much it MATTERS. Their existing glm52-mtp78-collector plugin is closer to the needed instrumentation than anything in vLLM proper.

claims.claim: EPLB's scratch buffer is allocated as torch.empty_like(w) against layer 0's weights, so it is byte-identical in shape, dtype, and size to the live weight tensors. It cannot hold a differently-sized payload.

claims.claim: Every EPLB weight movement is a fixed-shape row copy into a pre-existing destination: local staging is b[dst].copy_(w[src_local]), buffer drain is w[dst].copy_(b[dst]), and replica duplication is w[dst].copy_(w[src]). No allocation, no resize, no rebinding, no address change occurs anywhere in the path.

claims.claim: STRUCTURAL BLOCKER FOR PER-EXPERT MIXED PRECISION: FusedMoE.get_expert_weights() returns weight.view(local_num_experts, -1) for each parameter. Every expert in a layer is a row of ONE contiguous tensor with a uniform per-expert stride. A layer where expert 3 is K4 and expert 4 is K3 cannot be expressed in this layout at all — the view() would fail, and there is no per-expert storage to vary.

The background thread fills the buffer and sets ep_buffer_ready=1; the main thread drains it in move_to_workspace during the next step() and advances layer_to_transfer. The actual blocker for bit-width-varying weights sits one level below the wire: experts are rows of a single stacked (num_local_physical_experts, hidden_size_i) tensor (rebalance_execute.py:487-489, :598), and the swap buffers are allocated once as torch.empty_like of layer 0 under the note "we assume the same weights across different layers have the same shape" (rebalance_execute.py:605-610, eplb_state.py:481). Those two facts make per-expert and per-layer bit-width divergence impossible at EP=1, with no networking involved.

summary: In vLLM v1, a captured CUDA graph is an immutable recording with device pointers baked into its node parameters, and vLLM never re-captures after startup (capture_model has exactly one caller, gpu_worker.py:608, and capture is globally disabled afterwards at gpu_model_runner.py:5757 / monitor.py:86-95). Replacing a weight tensor at a NEW address silently breaks every graph that touched it: the address check at cuda_graph.py:338-347 runs only when VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL==DEBUG and only over positional args, not module parameters, so the failure mode is garbage output or an IMA, not an exception. Changing the SIZE is strictly worse: weights enter the compiled graph as placeholders with concrete (non-symbolic) shapes (backends.py:1186-1189), and vLLM deliberately drops ALL Dynamo guards (wrapper.py:105-120), so a shape/dtype/storage change never triggers a recompile — Inductor keeps launching the old kernels with the old strides. That is exactly why EPLB is safe: rearrange_expert_weights_inplace only ever does w[dst].copy_() into VIEWS of the original parameter storage (layer.py:1441-1450 returns weight.view(local_num_experts,-1); rebalance_execute.py:427,465) at identical shape and address. The same discipline governs the only two other runtime-mutation paths in the tree: layerwise reload copies processed values back into the original storage with the comment "preserves cudagraph refs" (layerwise.py:239-245), and LoRA hot-swap uses fixed-capacity preallocated stacked buffers with copy_ into a padded slot (lora/layers/base_linear.py:65-85,110-120). The one existing mechanism that changes a tensor's BACKING STORE without invalidating graphs is the CUDA VMM sleep/wake allocator: cuMemUnmap+cuMemRelease frees the physical pages but keeps the reserved virtual address, and wake_up cuMemMaps brand-new physical memory at the SAME d_mem (cumem.py:214,240-241; csrc/cumem_allocator.cpp:145,207-211,323,414) — that is the strongest lever for the fungible-quant idea, but the reservation is exactly alignedSize (csrc/cumem_allocator.cpp:319-323), so it buys new bits at a stable address, not a bigger tensor. In the GG fork the constraints are far harder than upstream: exl3.py bakes RAW DEVICE POINTERS into an int64 device tensor at load time (exl3.py:1534-1542, stored at 1810) and validates slab aliasing by data_ptr (exl3.py:1509-1530); a trellis tensor's last dim is literally 16*bits, so K3->K4 changes the SHAPE (exl3.py:1743-1762); the mixed K3/K4 path builds compact tier-ordered COPIES and keys its cached runtime on (bits,count) per tier, raising if that changes under capture (exl3.py:1616-1687, 1840-1863); and b12x destroys the source Parameters after preparing its own weight owner (b12x_moe.py:1004-1006, 1415-1430), so swapping layer.w13_weight would not even be read by the kernel. Answer to the central question: within a captured graph, stable-address plus fixed-capacity in-place mutation is the only safe weight swap, with exactly one escape hatch — VMM physical remapping behind a stable VA, which vLLM already ships for sleep/wake. Anything that changes tensor size requires the elastic-EP stop-the-world teardown (elastic_execute.py:389-414: drop all graph entries, torch.compiler.reset(), unlock workspace, full re-warmup and re-capture, re-lock). The practical design that survives all of this: fix the per-layer tier cardinalities at startup (|K4| = N, |K3| = E-N), allocate at the high-water geometry, and make rebalancing a membership SWAP executed as copy_ into a vacated slot — turning fungible quant into an EPLB-shaped problem instead of a reallocation problem.

summary:
vLLM's GPU memory model is a one-shot, closed budget computed once at startup and then frozen. `request_memory()` fixes a hard ceiling of `total_memory * gpu_memory_utilization`; `determine_available_memory()` measures weights, peak activation, non-torch and CUDA-graph memory once, and hands whatever is left to the KV cache, which is then materialized as monolithic `torch.zeros` allocations. There is no weight arena, no growable weight region, and no re-profiling path. After startup the only free bytes on the device are the deliberately *unrequested* slack `total*(1-util)` — memory vLLM treats as safety margin, not as budget. So a weight that grows by 1 GiB after startup does not "break" anything at the accounting layer, because nothing is watching: it silently eats the OOM safety margin, and once that margin is gone the failure surfaces as an OOM inside an arbitrary kernel (or inside CUDA-graph replay), not as a clean budget error. The KV cache is already fully allocated and cannot shrink to make room.

The EPLB precedent the idea leans on is real but narrower than hoped. `rearrange_expert_weights_inplace(is_profile=True)` genuinely pre-reserves its communication buffers during `profile_run` so the memory accounting is honest — that is a clean, copyable pattern for reserving swap headroom. But those buffers are `torch.empty_like(w)`: same shape, same size, forever. Nothing in vLLM — not EPLB, not `reload_weights` (`param.copy_`), not even elastic-EP scaling (which holds `num_local_experts` constant and adds *ranks*) — ever resizes a per-rank weight tensor. The one true precedent for runtime resizing is `WorkspaceManager` (grow → `lock()` after capture) and elastic EP's `unlock_workspace() → torch.compiler.reset() → recapture → lock_workspace()`, which is a full stop-the-world reconfiguration, not a hot swap.

The GG fork's "arena" is *not* a weight arena — it is the b12x Trellis activation scratch buffer (~1 GiB for the prefill plan), sized by token capacity, and it is the sharpest blocker in the whole design. Its runtime cache key includes `tier_signature` = ((3, n_K3), (4, n_K4)). Any K3↔K4 rebalance changes that signature, misses the cache, recompiles the megakernel, and allocates a *new* ~1 GiB arena into a global dict that never evicts. Worse, runtimes are scoped per *model*, not per layer, precisely because the fork's own docstring says per-layer arenas would cost "tens of GiB per rank on a 75+ layer model and are not affordable" — which means per-layer heterogeneous bit allocation, the entire point of a fungible quant, is exactly the thing the current arena design cannot afford. Two further hard walls: the mixed path requires *exactly two* bitrate tiers, and rank-sliced EXL3 checkpoints hard-fail if `checkpoint_tp != runtime tp`, so the format is already topology-baked, contradicting the topology-neutrality goal.

Arithmetic (H=6144, E=256, top-8, TP4; I=2048 and 77 MoE layers derived — they reproduce 744.1B routed params exactly, and the EXL3 slab shapes give byte-exact bpw): one expert in one layer K3→K4 costs 1.125 MiB/GPU (4.5 MiB across 4 GPUs). One expert index across all 77 layers costs 86.6 MiB/GPU. All-K3 → all-K4 costs 21.66 GiB/GPU. Each +0.01 of routed bpw costs 221.8 MiB/GPU, and the 3.0→3.42 bpw spread the user already runs is 9.10 GiB/GPU. The killer is granularity: because tier slabs are contiguous stacked tensors, moving *one* expert forces a rebuild of *both* tier slabs for that layer — ~0.96 GiB/rank, ~1.92 GiB/rank double-buffered — and the per-expert source tensors are deliberately freed at load time, so there is nothing on-device to re-stack from.

Viable path: the fork already ships two of the three pieces needed. `_reserve_mm_ipc_gpu_memory()` is a working precedent for carving a fixed reserve out of `available_kv_cache_memory_bytes`, and `startup_plan.py` is a working precedent for a fingerprinted, cached, rehydrated-at-boot memory plan. Size the budget for K_max and under-fill for K3 — pay for the worst case up front, spend the slack later.
